extracted.intended_audience: short story writers, literary editors, and readers interested in short-fiction craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and editorial criteria for selecting and writing short stories (including discussion of novellas, trends, venues, and what makes a story have impact). Draws on editors' foreword and selection rationale for an annual anthology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short story length (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A short story is a story that is not too long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The only satisfactory definition the editor quotes is: 'A short story is a story that is not too long.' If a story is very long and interesting it could be called a novel; there is also an intermediate form (novella).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plot-first composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should not begin by inventing a plot and pigeonholing characters into it; instead start with people, their emotions and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor criticizes the 'plot-first' approach: 'the dirtiest four-letter word a writer can use is plot.' 'Every real writer I ever knew... starts with people and their emotions and actions and lets them make their own stories.' Characters should drive the story rather than being forced into an invented plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters and interior life drive fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong fiction starts from characters, their emotions and actions; characters can 'make the author do what they want him to do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes starting with people and letting their interior life and behavior create the story. The anecdote about a would‑be student wanting to 'be like God and make people do what I want them to do' is used to warn against authorial imposition; instead authors must discover characters' needs and let them dictate events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write from one's knowing and feeling (authentic experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should 'write out of [their] own knowing and feeling' rather than inventing unfamiliar experience for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor recounts admonishing a would‑be contributor: 'Why in hell don’t you write out of your own knowing and feeling!' An example: an iron puddler's vivid writing of foundry life led to publishable stories. Grounding fiction in real experience yields vividness and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabulation vs. reality — balance required
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure invention divorced from reality (the 'fabulators') risks lacking impact and being easily forgotten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques the 'fabulators' who 'are trying to divorce their writing from all reality, to make it pure invention.' The editor finds such writing often lacks impact and is the 'most easily forgotten writing I have ever read.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Even fantastic writing should start from something real
rubrics_metrics.description: Even fantasy and science fiction are strongest when they begin with something real the author experienced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Ray Bradbury: 'all his stories, even those considered the most fantastic, started with something real he himself had experienced.' This supports using real emotional or experiential kernels as anchors for speculative or fantastic narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novella: length and character
rubrics_metrics.description: A novella is longer than a short story and shorter than a novel; it need not be 'pointed and compact' and may have a relaxed, expansive style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor objects to a dictionary definition that calls a novella 'a story with a pointed and compact plot,' noting canonical novellas (Ethan Frome, Heart of Darkness, The Bear) are not necessarily 'pointed or compact.' Many editors cannot publish novellas due to space limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trends are cycles — don't chase novelty for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: So‑called new trends in writing are often cyclical revivals; writers should not pursue trends solely because they are fashionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor views many 'trends' as revivals (e.g., black humor, concretism) and suggests these are cycles rather than genuine linear progress; implication: focus on craft and substance rather than fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation with form/typography (concretism) — use with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Typography and visual form can be integral to a piece, but extreme concretism (omitting language entirely) risks reducing meaning and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes about concretism: attempts to make typography part of reading matter can be interesting, but examples that omit language (an issue of the Chicago Review with no words) are taken as an extreme; experimentation should serve the reader and the work's effect rather than be novelty for novelty's sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frankness in sexual description and profanity is acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit sexual description and the use of four‑letter words are not inherently disqualifying; censorship objections are dated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor affirms: 'Absolutely' in response to whether authors continue to be uninhibited in sexual description and four‑letter words, noting historical context (Ulysses smuggling) and skepticism about claims that such language 'has evil influence on children.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication venue quality matters — 'little magazines' often excel
rubrics_metrics.description: Small‑circulation ('little') magazines frequently publish work of high literary quality even if they lack wide distribution or marketing budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor praises 'little' magazines as not little in quality and laments that many readers lack access to them; contrasts these with mass‑circulation magazines which may prioritize money over literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and distance for war stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Good war stories rarely coincide with the war in which they take place; perspective and historical distance often strengthen wartime fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor notes it is 'too soon' for good Vietnam war stories and that good war stories seldom arise during the conflict itself; often writers need distance (e.g., the Forties are only now being addressed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection favors strongly portrayed, unforgettable characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories selected emphasize strongly portrayed, unforgettable characters engaged with living and relating to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the anthology blurb: readers will 'discover many strongly portrayed, unforgettable characters, involved in various ways with the problems of living and relating to other people.' Selection thus privileges character depth and relational complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic resonance: family, aging, disillusionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that explore family situations, difficulties of communication, aging, loss of innocence, disillusionment with self/world, and struggles to keep pride are especially represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editors observe that 'Many of this year’s selections deal with family situations' (father‑son communication, a child's awareness of evil, attempts to keep illusions, pain of growing old, struggle to keep pride). These themes are highlighted as exemplary of the year's notable fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection should represent recent developments in the genre
rubrics_metrics.description: An anthology's chosen stories should 'represent to highest advantage the recent development of this particular literary genre.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editors assert their selections 'brought together twenty of the finest short stories of the past year — works which represent to highest advantage the recent development of this particular literary genre.' This implies curatorial criteria: quality plus representativeness of trends/themes/styles from the year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine editorial standards influence story quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial attitudes and commercial goals of magazines affect what kinds of stories they publish; some large magazines prioritize circulation and profit over literary quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique that some mass‑circulation magazines are 'primarily interested only in money and not in literature' and that women's magazines have 'been going downhill' for story quality. Editors should be aware of venue biases when scouting or submitting stories.
